rail_guard.text: Dover Priory. Trains to London, Canterbury and everywhere you've been. Boats are down the hill.
All aboard! Mind the gap, and the seagulls, in that order.

dv_ferry_fan.text: Ten thousand lorries a day through here, some days. Strawberries from Spain, cheese from France, car parts from everywhere.
When the port stops, Kent stops. They park the lorries on the motorway. Operation Stack, they called it. Nobody enjoyed it.

dv_birder.text: Kittiwakes! Hear them? They say their own name. Kitti-waaake. There are thousands on these cliffs every spring.
And there goes a fulmar: stiff wings, glides like a little albatross. They can spit a nasty oil at you if you get too near the nest. Ask me how I know.

dv_old_soldier.text: My dad was on a little ship at Dunkirk. A Thames pleasure boat, the sort you'd take to Margate for the day. He went back four times.
When he got home he never talked about it, except once, to say the beach went on for ever.

then.text: Thanks for helping out. Ramsay's map is back up, and the Harbourmaster's buying the teas.
In you go. Find the signaller on duty, then Admiral Ramsay's operations room at the back. Mind your head: the Napoleonic diggers were short.

else.text: {greeting} These tunnels were dug into the chalk in the Napoleonic Wars as barracks. In 1940 the Navy took them over.
It was here, in the cliffs, that Vice-Admiral Ramsay planned the Dunkirk evacuation. We're opening the operations room again, but the signals post has gone quiet and the map needs putting back.
Give us a hand? It's dark, so keep a light handy. Find our signaller first: she won't let anyone past without a challenge.

then.text: Dover, Wight, Portland, Plymouth. You've got it. Listen tonight at twelve minutes to one and you'll hear your own bit of sea read out.

else.text: {greeting} Thirty-one sea areas round these isles, and the Shipping Forecast reads every one in the same order, several times a day on the wireless. Viking to start, up by Norway, then clockwise round the coast, and Southeast Iceland to finish.

Each area gets three things: the wind, the weather, the visibility. 'Dover: southwesterly 5 to 7, occasionally gale 8 later. Rain. Moderate or poor.' Direction and force, then what's falling, then how far you can see. Gale is force 8 on the Beaufort scale, which an Irishman from Meath drew up for the Navy in 1805.
Quick test, since you're standing on the beach. No prizes but the knowing.
Which sea area are you standing in right now?

then.text: Dover, of course. Thames is next door to the east, Wight to the west. The names run clockwise round the coast.

else.text: You're in Dover. The town, the strait and the sea area. Thames is the next one east, Wight the next one west.

options: Force 8 wind on the Beaufort scale

then.text: Force 8, a gale: thirty-four knots and more. Twigs come off the trees and you can't walk straight. Force 12 is a hurricane.

else.text: It's the wind: force 8 on Beaufort's scale, a gale. Force 12 is a hurricane. The waves are somebody else's department.
One sea area was renamed in 2002, after the man who started the Met Office. Which?

then.text: FitzRoy. He captained the Beagle, founded the Met Office, and sent the first gale warnings in 1861. Finisterre's off Spain, and the Spanish had an area of that name already.

else.text: It was Finisterre, off the corner of Spain, renamed FitzRoy after the Beagle's captain who founded the Met Office and sent the first gale warnings in 1861.
That'll do. One more thing: 'imminent' means within six hours, 'soon' is six to twelve, 'later' is after that. People plan their lives round those words. Off you go, and mind the ferry.
